slides.title: Leukaemias: general concept and pathogenetic features
bullets: Leukaemia is a malignant tumour of haemopoietic cells arising from bone-marrow stem cells; tumour cells enter the peripheral blood, so the leukocyte count is usually high.
Tumour cells first multiply in the blood-forming organs (bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes), then spread haematogenously to other organs and form leukaemic infiltrates.
Leukaemias have many causes: ionising radiation, viruses, blastogenic chemicals and hereditary pathology lead to mutation of haemopoietic cells.

slides.title: Leukaemias: general concept and pathogenetic features
bullets: To diagnose leukaemia, four pathogenetic features must be found: hyperplasia, metaplasia, anaplasia and heterotopic foci where pathological blood cells form.

By the number of leukaemic cells in the blood, forms are distinguished: leukaemic, subleukaemic, leukopenic (few leukocytes but leukaemic cells in the blood) and aleukaemic (no leukaemic cells found in the blood).
Consequences: anaemia, haemorrhagic syndrome, deep dystrophic changes in parenchymal organs; reduced immunity leads to ulcerative-necrotic changes and sepsis.

slides.title: Groups of chronic leukaemias (traditional classification)
bullets: Chronic leukaemias are grouped by cell line: myelocytic, lymphocytic and monocytic.
Myelocytic leukaemias: chronic myeloid leukaemia, erythraemia (Vaquez disease) and others.
Lymphocytic leukaemias: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, cutaneous lymphomatosis (Sézary disease), paraproteinaemic leukaemias (including myeloma) and primary macroglobulinaemia.
Monocytic leukaemias: chronic monocytic leukaemia and histiocytoses.

slides.title: Groups of chronic leukaemias (traditional classification)
bullets: Paraproteinaemic leukaemias arise from cells of the B-lymphocytic system; their common feature is the ability to make paraprotein, and the most important is myeloma.
Chronic forms may run a relatively benign course for a long time; the author uses the traditional morphological classification.

slides.title: Telling leukaemia from leukaemoid reaction and similar conditions
bullets: In inflammatory and infectious diseases many young (blast) cells may appear in the blood and raise suspicion of leukaemia — this is a leukaemoid reaction.
It resembles leukaemia only through the rise in leukocytes and the appearance of young forms; metaplasia, anaplasia and heterotopic blood formation are absent.
These patients have signs of a tumour, sepsis or an inflammatory-infectious disease; the reaction passes once the underlying disease is found and treated.

slides.title: Telling leukaemia from leukaemoid reaction and similar conditions
bullets: In osteomyelosclerosis (myelofibrosis) there are also leukocytosis, enlarged liver and spleen, anaemia and young cells; marrow fibrosis shows in the trephine, and the anaplasia, metaplasia and heterotopic foci typical of leukaemia are absent.
Alkaline phosphatase (phosphomonoesterase I) activity in mature neutrophils is measured cytochemically: it is raised in a leukaemoid reaction and lowered in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

slides.title: Leukemias, etiology, pathogenesis and classification?
bullets: 1. Leukemias are clonal neoplastic diseases of hematopoietic cells; they begin in the bone marrow and spill into the blood.

2. Etiology/risk factors: ionizing radiation, benzene, prior chemotherapy, genetic syndromes (Down), prior MDS/MPN; pathogenesis – genetic alterations (translocations, mutations), for example t(9;22) BCR::ABL1, t(15;17) PML::RARA.

3. Classification: acute (blasts predominate) and chronic (mature cells predominate); myeloid and lymphoid; the current standard is WHO 5th edition (2022) and ICC 2022: types defined genetically and by differentiation.

slides.title: Leukemias, etiology, pathogenesis and classification?
bullets: 4. Diagnostic work-up: CBC and smear, bone marrow aspirate/trephine biopsy, cytochemistry, flow cytometry (immunophenotype), cytogenetics, FISH and molecular tests (PCR, NGS).
5. In acute myeloid leukemia the classical threshold is ≥20% blasts in blood or bone marrow; in WHO-2022 this threshold has been removed for most genetically defined types.

slides.title: Acute leukemias. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in acute leukemias?
bullets: 1. Acute leukemia is clonal proliferation of immature blast cells and suppression of normal hematopoiesis.

2. Peripheral blood: anemia (normocytic), thrombocytopenia, leukocytes increased, normal or decreased; blasts (high nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, fine chromatin, nucleoli); "leukemic hiatus" – no intermediate forms between blasts and mature cells.
3. Bone marrow: hypercellular, many blasts – ≥20% for AML (in some genetic types the threshold is lower/absent); normal lineages suppressed.

slides.title: Acute leukemias. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in acute leukemias?
bullets: 4. Identifying the myeloid type: Auer rods, myeloperoxidase positivity; in APL promyelocytes with many Auer rods and the risk of DIC – an emergency.
5. Confirmation: flow cytometry (myeloid/B/T lineage), cytogenetics and molecular tests (for example t(15;17) PML::RARA, FLT3, NPM1) – for classification and prognosis.
6. Remission: <5% blasts in the bone marrow, recovery of blood counts.

slides.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture?
bullets: 1. CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm; in ~90–95% of patients t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, the BCR::ABL1 fusion protein (mainly p210) – a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.

2. Peripheral blood (chronic phase): marked leukocytosis, granulocytes of all maturation stages (many myelocytes and segmented forms – "two-peak" distribution), basophilia and eosinophilia, blasts <2%, platelets often increased.
3. Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular, hyperplasia of the granulocytic lineage, small megakaryocytes; Ph+ cytogenetics.

slides.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture?
bullets: 4. Phases: chronic → accelerated (increase in blasts and basophils) → blast crisis (myeloid or lymphoid).
5. Confirming the diagnosis: cytogenetics or FISH (t(9;22)), RT-PCR (BCR::ABL1); monitoring treatment – quantitative RT-PCR (molecular response).
6. Difference from a leukemoid reaction: basophilia, BCR::ABL1 positivity, clonality.
